channel.title: Oddly Wired
channel.description: One checked psychology fact a day. Every claim names the study behind it.

item.title: You remember stories better than raw information.
item.description: A 1969 study by Bower and Clark showed that readers remembered information significantly better when it was framed as a narrative.

item.title: You believe you can influence outcomes based on pure chance.
item.description: A 1975 study found that people were willing to bet more money on a game of luck if they were the ones rolling the dice.

item.title: The presence of more people makes you less helpful.
item.description: Darley and Latané (1968) found participants were 85% likely to help a person in need when alone, and 31% when four others were present.

item.title: You assume other people agree with your personal views.
item.description: Ross, Greene, and House (1977) found that participants who agreed to walk around with a 'Repent' sign believed approximately 63.5% of their peers would do the same.

item.title: You value items higher simply because you own them.
item.description: A 1990 study found participants were willing to pay $3.50 for a mug, but demanded $7.00 to part with it.

item.title: You overestimate your ability to manage your future moods.
item.description: Projection bias is the tendency to assume your future self will have the same tastes, desires, and emotional states as your current self.

item.title: Your expectation of an outcome can trigger a real result.
item.description: The placebo effect demonstrates that physiological responses can be altered by your beliefs about a treatment, even if the treatment is inert.

item.title: You look to strangers to decide which path is correct.
item.description: Asch's (1951) study showed that participants gave incorrect answers in approximately one-third (35.7%) of trials to match the consensus, though the majority of responses remained correct.

item.title: You rewrite your values to justify actions you already took.
item.description: Festinger's theory posits that when behavior conflicts with beliefs, individuals are motivated to reduce the resulting dissonance by employing various strategies, which may include changing beliefs, altering behavior, or adding new information.

item.title: You rewrite your memory to claim you saw it coming.
item.description: Fischhoff (1975) demonstrated that after an event occurs, people consistently overestimate their ability to have predicted the outcome.

item.title: You judge a stranger's intelligence solely by their appearance.
item.description: Thorndike (1920) found that people consistently attribute positive traits to individuals who possess one unrelated positive characteristic.

item.title: Your first impression of a price sets the internal standard.
item.description: Tversky and Kahneman found that participants' estimates of unknown quantities are consistently pulled toward an arbitrary starting number.

item.title: You adjust your confidence to match your social environment.
item.description: The spotlight effect is the psychological tendency to believe you are being noticed more than you actually are.

item.title: You suffer more when success is almost within reach.
item.description: The Medvec et al. (1995) study found that silver medalists are less satisfied than bronze medalists due to upward counterfactual thinking focused on the missed gold medal.

item.title: You assume a person's current mood is their permanent nature.
item.description: The correspondence bias is a common, though not universal, tendency to infer stable personality traits from observed behavior, even when that behavior is driven by the situation.

item.title: You value things more just because you suffered for them.
item.description: Effort justification is a specific paradigm derived from cognitive dissonance theory, most notably demonstrated by Aronson and Mills in 1959.

item.title: You have stopped remembering things because the internet does.
item.description: The Google effect, or digital amnesia, is the tendency to forget information that can be easily accessed via search engines.

item.title: You choose the middle option because it looks balanced.
item.description: The compromise effect is the tendency to avoid extremes when choosing between items, favoring the option that sits in the middle of a presented range.

item.title: You fail to notice the obvious in plain sight.
item.description: Inattentional blindness occurs when an individual fails to perceive an unexpected stimulus in plain sight because their attentional resources are fully occupied by a concurrent task.

item.title: You see biases in others but never in yourself.
item.description: The bias blind spot is the tendency to identify the cognitive biases of others more readily than one's own.

item.title: You expect good things to happen to you disproportionately.
item.description: The optimism bias is a cognitive illusion where you believe you are less at risk of negative events and more likely to experience positive outcomes than your peers.

item.title: You remember your past choices as better than they were.
item.description: Choice-supportive bias is the tendency to retroactively attribute positive attributes to an option you selected and negative attributes to those you rejected.

item.title: You think your personality is finished developing today.
item.description: The end-of-history illusion shows people recognize they have changed in the past but mistakenly believe they will remain mostly static in the future.

item.title: You see patterns in noise that are not actually there.
item.description: A 1967 study showed that clinicians perceived correlations between personality traits and drawing styles that were completely absent from the data.

item.title: You remember the beginning and the end, not the middle.
item.description: A 1962 study found that in lists of words, participants recalled the items at the beginning and end significantly better than the middle.

item.title: You prefer a smaller reward now over a larger one later.
item.description: A 1975 study found that the subjective value of a reward decreases hyperbolically as the delay to receive it increases.

item.title: Holding a warm drink makes you judge strangers as warmer.
item.description: A 2008 study reported that participants holding warm coffee judged a target person to have a 'warmer' personality, but this finding has failed to replicate in larger, independent studies.

item.title: You want a thing more precisely because it is forbidden.
item.description: Research by Jack Brehm in 1966 suggests that restricting your freedom to choose leads to a sudden increase in the perceived value of the unavailable option.

item.title: You eventually forget where you heard the information.
item.description: In a 1951 study, participants who dismissed a message due to an untrustworthy source began to agree with the message weeks later.

item.title: You consume the entire portion regardless of the amount.
item.description: Unit bias is the tendency to consume a single discrete unit of an item (such as one brownie or one scoop) regardless of its size, whereas the phenomenon of consuming more due to larger plates is known as the portion size effect.

item.title: The same information changes your choice depending on context.
item.description: The framing effect refers to the tendency for decisions to be influenced by whether information is presented as a gain or a loss relative to a reference point.

item.title: You blame your own mistakes on your situation.
item.description: The actor-observer asymmetry describes a general tendency to attribute your own behavior to situational factors while attributing the behavior of others to their internal character.

item.title: You assume experts share your clarity of thought.
item.description: The curse of knowledge is a cognitive bias where you find it difficult to imagine what it is like not to know what you know.

item.title: You get more done by pairing chores with treats.
item.description: Temptation bundling increases adherence to difficult tasks by combining them with immediate gratification.

item.title: You sell winning investments while keeping your losing ones.
item.description: The disposition effect is the tendency of investors to sell winning positions too early and hold onto losing positions too long.

item.title: Doing one good deed makes you act more selfishly.
item.description: Moral licensing occurs when performing a virtuous action provides a psychological credit that you spend on later behavior.

item.title: You think your inner emotions are obvious to others.
item.description: In a 1998 study, participants drastically overestimated the extent to which observers could detect their internal states.

item.title: You believe that your future self will stay the same.
item.description: The projection bias leads individuals to overestimate the degree to which their future tastes and needs will resemble their current state.

item.title: You are less likely to help if others are around.
item.description: The bystander effect occurs when the presence of others inhibits your individual urge to intervene in an emergency.

item.title: You find vague personality descriptions surprisingly accurate.
item.description: The Forer effect is the tendency for people to accept broad personality assessments as uniquely applicable to them.

item.title: You prefer the way things are by default.
item.description: The status quo bias describes the tendency to maintain a current state because the potential losses of changing are perceived as greater than the benefits, a concept driven by loss aversion.

item.title: You believe you contributed more than others did.
item.description: The egocentric bias leads you to overestimate your own input in collaborative efforts.

item.title: You give too much weight to a specific detail.
item.description: When evaluating life satisfaction, people tend to focus on a single piece of information while ignoring the larger context.

item.title: You seek unnecessary information before making simple choices.
item.description: Individuals often request extra information before deciding, even when that information has no impact on the outcome.

item.title: You overestimate risks that appear frequently in the news.
item.description: People judge the probability of an event by how easily they can recall similar instances from memory.

item.title: An anecdote outweighs data when you make a judgment.
item.description: You consistently prioritize specific, vivid information over broader, more accurate statistical trends.

item.title: Your brain goes blind for a moment after focusing.
item.description: When two targets are processed rapidly in an RSVP task, the probability of detecting the second target is significantly reduced if it appears within 200 to 500 milliseconds of the first.

item.title: Your first impression of a number dictates your judgment.
item.description: The initial, often arbitrary value you are presented with exerts a pull on all subsequent estimates.

item.title: Your memory rewrites past events to make them predictable.
item.description: Once you know the outcome of an event, you tend to overestimate the likelihood that you would have predicted that specific outcome beforehand.

item.title: You think you are more unique than you actually are.
item.description: A 1981 study found that most drivers rate themselves as safer and more skilled than the average driver.
